blocks.content: 1.1 Ancient History

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The ancient period of Telangana history is marked by the Satavahana Dynasty (230 BCE – 220 CE) and the Ikshvaku Dynasty.
The medieval period saw powerful regional powers including the Kakatiyas (1083–1323 CE) and the Qutb Shahi Dynasty (1518–1687 CE).
Hyderabad State under the Nizam Rule spanned from 1724 to 1948 until its integration into India.
The Telangana Armed Struggle occurred between 1946 and 1951 as a movement against local feudalism.
Following the Gentlemen's Agreement of 1956 and persistent agitation, Telangana achieved statehood in 2014.

blocks.content: Telangana is one of the oldest inhabited regions of the Indian subcontinent. Archaeological evidence found in places like Kurnool Caves and the Godavari river valley suggests human habitation dating back to the Stone Age. The Deccan Plateau, on which Telangana sits, has been witness to numerous civilizations over thousands of years.
1.1.1 Prehistoric Period

Excavations at sites like Nagarjunakonda, Amaravathi, and along the Krishna and Godavari rivers have revealed Neolithic and Megalithic cultures. The megalithic burial sites found in Telangana are among the most significant in South Asia. Pottery, iron implements, and ornaments excavated from these sites reflect the sophisticated nature of early Telangana civilization.
1.1.2 Satavahana Dynasty (230 BCE – 220 CE)

The Satavahanas, also known as the Andhras, were the first major dynasty to rule over the Telangana region. Their empire extended from the present-day states of Maharashtra to Andhra Pradesh. The Satavahana rulers were great patrons of Buddhism and built many stupas and viharas. Prominent rulers include:

items: Simuka – Founder of the Satavahana dynasty
Satakarni I – Expanded the kingdom significantly
Gautamiputra Satakarni – The greatest Satavahana ruler; defeated the Shakas and Kushanas
Yajna Sri Satakarni – Last notable ruler of the dynasty

blocks.content: Important Buddhist sites from the Satavahana era include Nagarjunakonda, Amaravathi, and Bhattiprolu. The Satavahanas developed a rich culture and contributed to the development of the Telugu language.
1.1.3 Ikshvaku Dynasty (3rd–4th Century CE)

After the Satavahanas, the Ikshvaku dynasty ruled the Krishna-Guntur region. They were also Buddhist patrons and built magnificent stupas at Nagarjunakonda (present-day Andhra Pradesh, but historically linked to Telangana's cultural sphere). The site was submerged when the Nagarjuna Sagar Dam was built, but artifacts are preserved on an island.
1.1.4 Vakataka and Pallava Influence

The Vakatakas (3rd–5th century CE) and later the Pallavas had significant influence over parts of Telangana. The Vakatakas were known for their patronage of Sanskrit literature and Hindu temple architecture.
1.2 Medieval History
1.2.1 Chalukyas of Badami (6th–8th Century CE)

The Chalukyas of Badami extended their control over parts of Telangana. The Chalukya ruler Pulakesi II defeated the Pallava king Mahendravarman I and controlled much of South India. Badami Chalukya architecture influenced temple building in Telangana.
1.2.2 Rashtrakutas (8th–10th Century CE)

The Rashtrakutas succeeded the Chalukyas and were great patrons of art and culture. Under rulers like Dantidurga and Krishna I (who built the Kailasanatha Temple at Ellora), Deccan culture flourished. Their territory included parts of present-day Telangana.
1.2.3 Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (973–1189 CE)

The Chalukyas of Kalyani (also called Later Chalukyas) had their capital at Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan in Karnataka). They ruled much of the Deccan including Telangana. Notable rulers: Tailapa II (founder), Vikramaditya VI (the greatest ruler who patronized the poet Bilhana and mathematician Vijnaneshwara).
1.2.4 Kakatiyas (1083–1323 CE)

The Kakatiyas are the most celebrated rulers of Telangana. They ruled from Warangal (Orugallu) and were instrumental in developing a distinct Telangana identity. The Kakatiya rulers unified the Telugu-speaking people and created a powerful empire.
Key Kakatiya Rulers:

cells: Greatest Kakatiya ruler; built Warangal Fort; extended empire to coast
One of very few female rulers in medieval India; mentioned by Marco Polo
Last Kakatiya ruler; defeated by Delhi Sultanate

blocks.content: Kakatiya Architecture and Achievements:

items: Warangal Fort – A massive fortress with four ornamental gateways (Kakatiya Kala Thoranam / Warangal Gate)
Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda – Built by Rudra Deva in 1163 CE
Ramappa Temple at Palampet – Built by Recharla Rudra in 1213 CE; recognized as UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021
Pakhal, Ramappa, Laknavaram Lakes – Engineering marvels built for irrigation
Development of Telugu literature and Shiva worship (Shaivism)

blocks.content: 1.2.5 Delhi Sultanate and Bahmani Period (1323–1518 CE)

In 1323 CE, Muhammad bin Tughluq of the Delhi Sultanate defeated Prataparudra II and annexed Telangana. However, Delhi's control weakened, and the Musunuri Nayaks revolted and temporarily freed Warangal (1336–1368 CE). Subsequently, the Bahmani Sultanate rose to power and controlled Telangana.
Police Action (Operation Polo) – 1948
The Bahmani Sultanate (1347–1527 CE) was founded by Hasan Gangu Bahman Shah. It was later divided into five Deccan Sultanates:

items: Bijapur Sultanate (Adil Shahis)
Ahmadnagar Sultanate (Nizam Shahis)
Bidar Sultanate (Barid Shahis)
Berar Sultanate (Imad Shahis)
Golconda Sultanate (Qutb Shahis)

blocks.content: 1.2.6 Qutb Shahi Dynasty – Golconda Sultanate (1518–1687 CE)
The Qutb Shahis ruled from Golconda and Hyderabad and are one of the most significant dynasties in Telangana's history. Sultan Quli Qutb Shah founded the dynasty in 1518. Key contributions:

items: Construction of Golconda Fort – An architectural marvel and a major diamond trading center
Founded Hyderabad city in 1591 CE by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah
Built Charminar (1591 CE) to commemorate the end of plague
Mecca Masjid – Built by Muhammad Qutb Shah, completed under Aurangzeb
Development of Urdu and Telugu literature; the rulers were themselves poets
Golconda was world-famous for diamonds – the Kohinoor, Hope Diamond, and Regent Diamond came from Golconda mines

blocks.content: 1.2.7 Mughal Rule (1687–1724 CE)

Aurangzeb besieged Golconda for eight months and finally captured it in 1687 CE after a traitor opened the gates. Telangana came under direct Mughal rule. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, the Mughal Empire weakened rapidly.
1.3 Hyderabad State and the Nizam Period (1724–1948)
1.3.1 Foundation of Hyderabad State

Mir Qamar-ud-Din Khan Siddiqi, better known as Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I, was the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan. He founded the Asaf Jah dynasty in 1724 CE and established Hyderabad as an independent state (though nominally under Mughal suzerainty).
The Nizams of Hyderabad:

cells: Last Nizam; once called the richest man in the world

blocks.content: 1.3.2 Nizam-British Relations

The Nizam of Hyderabad signed the Subsidiary Alliance with the British in 1798. Under this treaty, the Nizam maintained an internal autonomous status while British troops were stationed in Hyderabad. This made Hyderabad the largest princely state under British paramountcy. The Nizam received the title of 'Faithful Ally of the British Government.'
1.3.3 Salar Jung I and Modernization

Mir Turab Ali Khan, known as Salar Jung I, served as the Prime Minister of Hyderabad (1853–1883) under Nizam V and VI. He is credited with the modernization of Hyderabad State. His contributions include:

items: Restructuring of the administration and judiciary
Introduction of postal and telegraph services
Land revenue reforms
Establishment of schools and colleges
Built the Salar Jung Museum, now one of the largest one-man collections in the world

blocks.content: 1.3.4 Osmania University and Modern Hyderabad
Nizam VII, Mir Osman Ali Khan, was a significant modernizer despite his authoritarian rule. Key developments:

items: Founded Osmania University (1918) – the first university in India with Urdu as the medium of instruction
Built the Hyderabad High Court, City College, and Nizamia Hospital
Established the Nizam's State Railway
Built the Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar reservoirs
Constructed the Nizamabad-Secunderabad Railway

blocks.content: 1.3.5 Razakar Movement

The Razakars were a paramilitary force under Qasim Razvi, led under the banner of the Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (MIM). They opposed the merger of Hyderabad with India and carried out violence against Hindus and those favouring integration. The Razakars terrorized large parts of Telangana from 1947 to 1948.
1.3.6 Police Action (Operation Polo) – 1948

After India's independence on August 15, 1947, the Nizam of Hyderabad refused to accede to India and sought independent status. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, India's Home Minister, ordered military action. On September 17, 1948, the Indian Army launched 'Operation Polo' (also called the Police Action). Within five days, the Hyderabad State surrendered and was integrated into India. September 17 is celebrated as Telangana Liberation Day.
1.4 Telangana Armed Struggle (1946–1951)

Parallel to the Nizam and Razakar oppression, the people of Telangana rose in an armed peasant rebellion against the feudal system (Vetti/forced labor, deshmukhs, and Nizam's rule). This was led largely by the Communist Party of India (CPI).

items: The struggle began in Palakurthi (Nalgonda district) in July 1946
Thousands of peasants were mobilized under leaders like Ravi Narayana Reddy
The movement abolished Vetti (bonded labor), redistributed land, and established village governance
After the Police Action (1948), the Indian Army continued operations against Communist guerrillas
The struggle ended with the elections of 1951–52

blocks.content: 1.5 States Reorganization and the Telangana Movement
1.5.1 States Reorganization Act, 1956

The States Reorganization Commission (SRC), headed by Justice Fazal Ali, submitted its report in 1955. The SRC recommended the merger of Telangana with Andhra State (formed in 1953) to form Andhra Pradesh. Despite reservations from Telangana leaders, Andhra Pradesh was formed on November 1, 1956. This date is celebrated as Andhra Pradesh Formation Day.
1.5.2 Gentlemen's Agreement (1956)

items: Chronology of rulers: Satavahanas, Kakatiyas, Qutb Shahis, and Asaf Jahis (Nizams).
Police Action (Operation Polo) in 1948 leading to Hyderabad State's merger with the Indian Union.
Significance of the Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) and the States Reorganization Act, 1956.
Milestones of the Telangana Movement: 1969 Agitation, 1972 Jai Andhra Movement, and 2014 Statehood formation.

blocks.content: Before the merger, leaders from both regions signed the Gentlemen's Agreement to protect Telangana's interests. Key provisions included:

items: Mulki Rules – Jobs in Telangana would be reserved for local residents (Mulkis)
Regional Committee for Telangana to oversee development
Equitable share in government jobs and resources
Hyderabad as the joint capital

blocks.content: 1.5.3 Telangana Agitation (1969)

Violations of the Gentlemen's Agreement led to the first major Telangana agitation in 1969. Students and youth took to the streets demanding a separate state. The agitation was led by T. Nagi Reddy, Channa Reddy, and others. Over 369 people were killed in police firing. The movement was suppressed but the demand persisted.
1.5.4 Jai Andhra Movement (1972)

In response, Seema-Andhra regions launched the 'Jai Andhra' movement demanding protection of their rights, particularly opposing the Mulki Rules. The Supreme Court upheld Mulki Rules but they were later removed, disappointing Telangana.
1.5.5 Revival of Telangana Movement (1990s–2000s)

The Telangana Rashtra Samithi (TRS) was formed on April 27, 2001 by K. Chandrashekar Rao (KCR). KCR launched a fast-unto-death in 2009, which galvanized the movement. On December 9, 2009, the Central Government announced the formation of Telangana state. However, the announcement was suspended following protests from Seema-Andhra.
1.5.6 Telangana Statehood (2014)

After years of agitation, protests, political negotiations, and the Srikrishna Committee report, the Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act was passed by Parliament in February 2014. The state of Telangana was officially formed on June 2, 2014, becoming India's 29th state. K. Chandrashekar Rao became the first Chief Minister.
Key facts about Telangana's formation:

items: Date of Formation: June 2, 2014
State Capital: Hyderabad (shared with Andhra Pradesh for 10 years)
First Governor: ESL Narasimhan
First Chief Minister: K. Chandrashekar Rao (TRS)
Number of Districts at formation: 10 (later expanded to 33 and then 31)
